389/Concepts/A-Theory-of-Fun.title: A Theory of Fun
389/Concepts/A-Theory-of-Fun.content:
Raph Koster (A Theory of Fun for Game Design): “fun” is a particular kind of pattern recognition that humans have evolved to be good at and feel rewarded for engaging in. Being able to look at a situation and predict the outcome of a certain action is a survival trait.
In Koster’s framework, all games are fundamentally about teaching the player how to play the game. When the patterns are exhausted — when there’s nothing left to learn — the fun ends.

389/Concepts/Affordances-of-Movement.title: Affordances of Movement
389/Concepts/Affordances-of-Movement.content:
How it feels to traverse the world. Designing a character controller is about deciding what the player can and can’t do — what speeds, what jumps, what stops, what slides. Those decisions are the player’s primary experience of the game, often more than story or mechanics.
Vehicles and other forms of Constrained Movement provide narrative justification for putting interesting limits on how the player moves, which create affordances on both the design side and the player side.

389/Concepts/Agency-and-Self-Efficacy.title: Agency and Self-Efficacy
389/Concepts/Agency-and-Self-Efficacy.content:
The feeling that you have the capability to effect change — the belief that what you do matters. Underneath every self-conscious emotion: if the player doesn’t feel agency, they won’t feel complicit, proud, guilty, or embarrassed about anything that happens.
Agency is subjective. A game can branch radically based on player choice, but if the player doesn’t notice their influence, they won’t feel it. Conversely, a game can make a player feel hugely agentic with relatively few real choices — as long as the feedback clearly indicates that the choices made a difference.

389/Concepts/Alice-in-Wonderland-as-Game.title: Alice in Wonderland as Game Precursor
389/Concepts/Alice-in-Wonderland-as-Game.content:
A scene from Alice in Wonderland: a high table, a bottle labeled “Drink me,” a key, a door too small to fit through. At first look it’s nonsense. Through trial and error, the elements connect, and logic emerges.
Many video game situations work this way: the player enters a room, makes sense of the space as a puzzle, and then solves it. When designers insert an Alice reference into a game, they’re signaling the player to take on that mindset — to move from incomprehension to understood, so that they can proceed.

389/Concepts/Anticipation-in-Games.title: Anticipation in Games
389/Concepts/Anticipation-in-Games.content:
Several distinct mechanisms create anticipation in games:

Dramatic situations. Gone Home — you know something has happened, you know the answer is in the attic. You anticipate the surprise.
Hidden information. Among Us — all players know information is being withheld and will be revealed at round’s end.
Imposed wait times. Roller Coaster Tycoon — research and construction take in-game time, and the reveal of a new ride is itself anticipatory.
Skill unlocks. God of War — the player anticipates a more powerful weapon, new mechanics, new animations.
Looming revelation. The Beginner’s Guide — the sense that something is wrong gradually builds across the second half.

Different from cinematic anticipation in that the player is usually doing something in the meantime — the wait is occupied.
Related

389/Concepts/Asset-Reuse-for-Illusion-of.title: Asset Reuse for Illusion of Variety
389/Concepts/Asset-Reuse-for-Illusion-of.content:
The whole forest in Firewatch — a game that’s largely about walking through a forest — uses only 23 tree models. Most of the visible woods are 14 of them, scaled, rotated, and angled to create the illusion of variety.
Scope-conscious art direction leans on this hard. A small library of well-chosen assets, deployed with intent, reads as a richer world than a sprawling pile of one-off models. Useful framing for any week-long prototype: pick fewer pieces, use them more.

389/Concepts/Character-Dilemmas.title: Character Dilemmas
389/Concepts/Character-Dilemmas.content:
When it isn’t the player who is faced with a dilemma, but a character — that’s a story.
Dilemmas put characters under pressure. They act, they change, and maybe learn something about themselves. Sometimes the dilemma is more meaningful than the outcome. The best film dilemmas have double impact: they make us feel, and they say something culturally specific (Sophie’s Choice, Get Out).
A pivot point from designing player choice toward designing character arc — and an early hint that game arcs and narrative arcs are different tools.

389/Concepts/Choices-—-Risk-Reward,-Buil.title: Choices — Risk Reward, Builds, Progression, Emotional Weight
389/Concepts/Choices-—-Risk-Reward,-Buil.content:
Four common shapes for meaningful choice in games:

Risk and reward — two paths of unequal challenge and outcome. Super Mario 64’s level paths: both lead to the same star, but one is dangerous and full of treasure.
Builds — a choice at the start of the game that affects your experience throughout. Mass Effect class, Hades weapon, Magic deck.
Progression — choices made during play that shape strategy and playstyle. Baldur’s Gate 3 level-up, Hades boons, Deus Ex tech tree.
Emotional weight — choices made difficult by dramatic context, even when the mechanics don’t change much. The Companion Cube in Portal exists for exactly this.

A single game can use any combination. Designing a choice well usually means picking which kind it is and making the stakes legible.

389/Concepts/Collaborative-Playtesting.title: Collaborative Playtesting
389/Concepts/Collaborative-Playtesting.content:
Sometimes it’s useful to have two playtesters, even when the game is a single-player experience. When two people play together — one steering, one helping — they have to talk to each other about what to do, and that conversation gives you valuable insight into what decisions they’re making and why.
Especially useful when your game has explicit decision points. Those moments naturally prompt discussion, and the discussion is the signal.

389/Concepts/Constrained-Movement.title: Constrained Movement
389/Concepts/Constrained-Movement.content:
Racing games, rail shooters, dark rides, minecart sections — all use vehicular conventions to lock the player onto a track. The constraint isn’t a limitation; it’s the design.
By taking degrees of freedom away from the player, the designer gains a richer set of affordances: cinematic camera moves, focused player attention, complex mechanics that don’t compete with navigation, and an environment built precisely for the path the player will take through it.

389/Concepts/Constraints-Create-Challeng.title: Constraints Create Challenge
389/Concepts/Constraints-Create-Challeng.content:
Another parable: golf is a game with the goal of putting a ball in a hole. That would be easy and boring if you could just pick it up and drop it in. The rules require you to stand far away and hit it with a stick.
The constraints create the challenge. The challenge creates the fun. A lot of design work is choosing which constraints to add so that the activity becomes worth doing — and which ones to remove so the activity stays accessible.

389/Concepts/Controlled-Perspective.title: Controlled Perspective
389/Concepts/Controlled-Perspective.content:
Dark rides — Disney’s Haunted Mansion, classic Pirates of the Caribbean — exploit the visitor’s constrained position to control pacing, stage surprises, and pull off visual tricks that only work from one angle: the hollow-mask illusion, infinity mirrors, Pepper’s ghost.
Games can do the same. Billboarded sprites in Cruis’n USA, parallax scrolling, and any “always-faces-the-camera” effect rely on the player not being able to walk around the trick. The constraint is what makes the illusion possible.

389/Concepts/Defining-Paths-and-Sightlin.title: Defining Paths and Sightlines
389/Concepts/Defining-Paths-and-Sightlin.content:
A level isn’t just a space — it’s a set of paths through the space, with focal points, sightlines, and bottlenecks shaping how the player moves. Shooter design has the most developed vocabulary for this (navigation point density, choke points, flow charts), but the ideas apply to any level you can walk through.
When you lay out a level, ask where the player’s eye will land first, what they’ll be drawn toward, where decisions happen, and where they have no choice but to pass.

389/Concepts/Design-Documentation-—-Trea.title: Design Documentation — Treatment, Macro, Specification
389/Concepts/Design-Documentation-—-Trea.content:
Three flavors of design documentation, each used for a different audience and moment in production:

Treatment — overview / executive summary. Enough for someone to understand the basic concept, with diagrams and wireframes. Used for onboarding and pitching.
Macro — production document. A spreadsheet with detailed scope, sequences, assets. Internal; used for planning. See The Macro.
Specification — the “classic” GDD. Long-form reference document, full of diagrams, tables, art bible / world bible / TDD. Hard to keep in sync with an iterative process; used mainly when you have to show publishers or investors the full thing.

Most studios live primarily in the macro.

389/Concepts/Designed-Experiences.title: Designed Experiences
389/Concepts/Designed-Experiences.content:
Media that are created to inspire a particular emotional reaction from their audience. Not just games — anthems, short films, comic strips, haunted houses. Each medium uses its own tools (sound, cinematography, graphic design, space design), but they’re all engineering for a specific felt outcome.
When you experience any kind of media, ask: what emotion is this designed to evoke, and how is it going about evoking it? That’s the same question you’ll ask of your own prototypes.

389/Concepts/Designing-Interesting-Choic.title: Designing Interesting Choices
389/Concepts/Designing-Interesting-Choic.content:
From Caleb Compton’s essay Designing Interesting Choices in Games (and when not to). Not every moment of choice produces an interesting one — many “choices” in games are formal (you can move left or right) without being meaningful (one is obviously better, or the consequences are invisible).
An interesting choice tends to have: real stakes, legible alternatives, visible consequences, and no obvious correct answer. When you’re designing one, check whether the player has the information they need to care about which option they pick.

389/Concepts/Divergent-Prototyping.title: Divergent Prototyping
389/Concepts/Divergent-Prototyping.content:
Once you’ve built a prototype that targets a specific question or emotion, the next move isn’t to refine it — it’s to try a completely different angle. Can you reach the same goal through narrative? Mechanics? Metaphor? Procedural rhetoric?
Divergent prototyping is what protects you from premature commitment. The second prototype isn’t there to be better; it’s there to not be the same. Then you compare what you learned from both before deciding what to build next.

389/Concepts/ELIZA-Effect.title: ELIZA Effect
389/Concepts/ELIZA-Effect.content:
When the player’s experience of a system suggests more complexity than the system actually has. Named for Joseph Weizenbaum’s 1966 chatbot ELIZA, whose simple pattern-matching led users to attribute understanding and even empathy to it.
Useful for designers — a small amount of carefully placed responsiveness can make a game world feel alive — but fragile. If the player interacts long enough to see how the machinery really works, the illusion collapses and they feel cheated. Compare with the Tale-Spin Effect, where surface output instead obscures a richer simulation underneath.

389/Concepts/Engines-of-Experience.title: Engines of Experience
389/Concepts/Engines-of-Experience.content:
From Tynan Sylvester, Designing Games, Chapter 1. Frames games as machines for producing emotional response, and offers a working list of emotional triggers designers can pull on:
learning, character arcs, challenge, social interaction, acquisition, music, spectacle, beauty, environment, technology, primal threats, sexual signals.
The list isn’t complete and isn’t meant to be — it’s a starting palette for thinking about what’s actually doing the work when a game makes you feel something.

389/Concepts/Evoking-vs-Depicting-Emotio.title: Evoking vs Depicting Emotion
389/Concepts/Evoking-vs-Depicting-Emotio.content:
There’s a difference between evoking an emotion and depicting one. A cinematic narrative game can portray a character going through grief — but that’s not the same as making the player feel grief.
When designing a prototype to target an emotion, the question isn’t what the characters feel; it’s what you feel as you play. That’s a higher bar, and it’s the bar 389’s emotion-focused assignments are aiming at.

389/Concepts/Explore-Exploit.title: Explore-Exploit
389/Concepts/Explore-Exploit.content:
From Algorithms to Live By (Brian Christian & Tom Griffiths), Chapter 2. The tension between searching for new information (explore) and using what you already know (exploit). Restaurants you’ve never tried vs. your favorite place. New game vs. the comfort replay.
Games are full of explore/exploit moments — open-world choice of next quest, risk-vs-known-path forks, draft picks, build decisions. Designing them well means knowing which side of the tension you’re tilting the player toward, and why.

389/Concepts/Five-Act-Structure.title: Five Act Structure
389/Concepts/Five-Act-Structure.content:
From Will Storr, The Science of Storytelling. A narrative arc framed as the protagonist’s transformation under pressure:

Act I — This is me, and it’s not working. The old theory of control is established. Change strikes.
Act II — Is there another way? The old theory breaks down. A new way is sensed and tested.
Act III — There is. I have transformed. The new strategy works. But the plot strikes back harder.
Act IV — But can I handle the pain of change? Lowest point. The protagonist questions whether to keep going.
Act V — Who am I going to be? Final battle. The dramatic question gets a definitive answer.

The five-act frame doesn’t fit every story (especially short films), but it’s a usable scaffold for thinking about how a character’s internal arc maps onto the external plot.

389/Concepts/Flip-the-Script.title: Flip the Script
389/Concepts/Flip-the-Script.content:
A vital design skill, rarely named: putting yourself in the shoes of someone who is encountering your work for the first time. As a designer, you have to think about what your game looks like to a brand-new player who knows nothing about it — even though you know everything about it.
The same skill applies to a portfolio. What does the reviewer want? How much time will they spend? What do they see in the first three seconds? Role-play your audience the way you’d playtest your game.

389/Concepts/Formal-Dramatic-Dynamic-Ele.title: Formal Dramatic Dynamic Elements
389/Concepts/Formal-Dramatic-Dynamic-Ele.content:
Tracy Fullerton’s frame (Game Design Workshop) for deconstructing games into three layers:

Formal — rules, procedures, objectives, resources, conflicts, boundaries, outcomes. The skeleton.
Dramatic — premise, characters, story, visual style. The flesh.
Dynamic — what emerges in actual play. Affordances and constraints producing experience.

Useful both for analyzing existing games and for being explicit with your own team about which layer you’re discussing.

389/Concepts/Four-Arcs-of-Experience.title: Four Arcs of Experience
389/Concepts/Four-Arcs-of-Experience.content:
The 389 semester spine. Four lenses for constructing and deconstructing games — each with its own toolkit:

Narrative arc — stories about characters who act and change under the pressure of dilemmas. Pacing built from small and large surprises. See Character Dilemmas, Five Act Structure, Small vs Large Surprises.
Mechanical arc — how the player relates to the player character and the world. Changing mechanics is how you make the player reevaluate their experience.
Subtext and theme — surrealist patterns of presenting illogic and inviting the player to make meaning. Metaphor as a key. See Subtext and Theme via Metaphor, Surrealism in Games.
Agency — self-efficacy and self-conscious emotion. Games can use feedback, Narrative Listening, and multiple endings to give players the sense their actions matter. See Agency and Self-Efficacy, Self-Conscious Emotions.

A game can use any combination. Most use several. This is the frame your prototypes are constructed and critiqued against.

389/Concepts/Keys-and-Doors.title: Keys and Doors
389/Concepts/Keys-and-Doors.content:
The most common obstacle pattern in games: something blocks the player’s progress, and something else (found, earned, or activated) removes the block. Doom and Pokémon use literal keys and doors. Portal uses companion cubes and pressure plates. The Last of Us uses generators and dumpsters — keys and doors dressed in narrative clothes.
Sometimes the “key” isn’t an object at all but a new ability the player has gained — Link’s hookshot, Ori’s double jump. The metroidvania genre is essentially keys-and-doors where every key is a verb.

389/Concepts/Less-is-More-—-AI-Complexit.title: Less is More — AI Complexity
389/Concepts/Less-is-More-—-AI-Complexit.content:
Players read complexity into surprisingly simple behaviors. The GDC talk on RocketsRocketsRockets makes this case clearly: enemies in that game follow rules that fit in a few lines, but players describe their behavior as cunning, cowardly, opportunistic — full of intention.
Good game AI usually doesn’t need to be sophisticated. It needs to be legible: behaviors that a player can pattern-match on, with enough variation to seem alive.

389/Concepts/Lost-Woods-as-Guided-Experi.title: Lost Woods as Guided Experience
389/Concepts/Lost-Woods-as-Guided-Experi.content:
The “Lost Woods” pattern: a maze space that feels disorienting but tells the player what to pay attention to — and that attention guides them through. The player can brute-force it, but doesn’t have to.
Ocarina of Time uses a sound cue. Breath of the Wild uses wind and torch flame. Alan Wake uses a flashlight in a dark forest. In each case the game gives the player a path to follow without flattening the sense of being somewhere mysterious.

389/Concepts/Mazes-—-Navigation-and-Trav.title: Mazes — Navigation and Traversal
389/Concepts/Mazes-—-Navigation-and-Trav.content:
Video games have a long history of using mazes as obstacles — but simple mazes are rarely satisfying. The brute-force maze (try every passage, draw a map, eventually get out) treats disorientation as the whole challenge. There’s not much nuance to the frustration, and not much satisfaction to rote memorization.
The alternative is the maze as a guided experience — a space where the player feels disoriented but is given enough cues (light, sound, landmarks, in-fiction tools) to navigate. The fun is the sense of mastery over a place that looks threatening.

389/Concepts/Narrative-Listening.title: Narrative Listening
389/Concepts/Narrative-Listening.content:
A term from Teddy Diefenbach’s 2012 MFA thesis project, The Moonlighters. A design technique where the game pays attention and responds to player actions at a level usually treated as noise — the small, off-task, antisocial, or exploratory behaviors most games ignore.
Chrono Trigger’s Millennial Fair sequence is a famous earlier example: the game silently records “ordinary RPG behavior” that gets used against the player in a later trial. When games listen at this level, the player’s sense of agency expands sharply.

389/Concepts/Parable-of-the-Clay-Pots.title: Parable of the Clay Pots
389/Concepts/Parable-of-the-Clay-Pots.content:
From David Bayles and Ted Orland, Art & Fear. A ceramics teacher divides the class in two: one half graded on quantity (pounds of pots produced), the other on quality (a single perfect pot). At the end of the semester, the highest-quality work comes from the quantity group — they had been making, and learning from their mistakes, while the quality group sat theorizing.
The takeaway for 389: make a lot of small things. Practice scoping, get them into engine quickly, and iterate. A pile of finished prototypes beats one half-built masterpiece.

389/Concepts/Parser-Based-Games.title: Parser-Based Games
389/Concepts/Parser-Based-Games.content:
Text adventures of the 1970s and 1980s — Zork, Adventure, and their descendants — where the player types commands (LOOK AT MIRROR, GO NORTH, TALK TO GUARD) and the game parses them against an internal model of the world.
In the 1990s and 2000s the form became a hobbyist and academic sandbox under the name interactive fiction: a testbed for experimental narrative that has quietly shaped modern adventure design, immersive sims, and puzzle/mystery games. Photopia, Galatea, Counterfeit Monkey. Worth playing one to feel the constraints work for a story rather than against it.

389/Concepts/Player-Attention.title: Player Attention
389/Concepts/Player-Attention.content:
How do you get the player to look at a particular thing? A viewer’s eye is drawn to:

Movement
The brightest object
The most saturated color
The most contrast
An actor’s eyes
Center of frame

Players also pay special attention to threats and interactables. In games, players are often working out what their task is and what the tools are for accomplishing it — directing their attention is how you guide them from feeling lost to feeling found.

389/Concepts/Portfolio-Design.title: Portfolio Design
389/Concepts/Portfolio-Design.content:
A portfolio is interactive media. Approach it as a design problem the same way you’d approach designing a game: start with the experience goal. What do you want a reviewer to understand about you after looking at it? How do you present your work to create that understanding?
Then Flip the Script — put yourself in the reviewer’s shoes. They have limited time, specific things they’re looking for, and no obligation to dig. Make the first few seconds count, and Show Your Process so the reader can see how you work, not just what you shipped.

389/Concepts/Precedents-and-Curation.title: Precedents and Curation
389/Concepts/Precedents-and-Curation.content:
Designers work from precedents. When you have an idea, the first move is usually to look for games that have done something adjacent — not to copy them, but to see what’s already been figured out and what still hasn’t.
If you can’t find a precedent, keep looking. A precedent doesn’t have to match what you’re trying to do exactly; it just has to share enough that you can learn from where it succeeded or fell short.
Your own Steam library, watched, played, and remembered, is one of your most important resources.

389/Concepts/Prisoner's-Dilemma-in-Games.title: Prisoner's Dilemma in Games
389/Concepts/Prisoner's-Dilemma-in-Games.content:
Games can use social pressure and game theory to manufacture difficult choices, especially when other players are involved. Dead Last is a tabletop game where two players split a pot of loot — each can take a small share or a large share, but if both go large, neither gets anything and the loot redistributes to everyone else. Zero Escape: Virtue’s Last Reward builds whole narrative arcs around the same structure.
The mechanic works because the “right” move depends on what you believe the other player will do — which makes the choice psychological, not just optimal.

389/Concepts/Problem-Solution-Ordering.title: Problem-Solution Ordering
389/Concepts/Problem-Solution-Ordering.content:
From Max Kreminski’s essay Locked doors, headaches, and intellectual need: when a game (or a teacher, or a salesperson) hands the player a solution before they understand the problem, the solution feels arbitrary. Aspirin works great when you have a headache — and seems ridiculous when you don’t.
Many key-and-door designs fail this way: the player picks up a tool with no friction yet, then walks into the obstacle it solves, and the whole interaction is hollow. The fix is to make the player want the solution — let them feel the problem first.

389/Concepts/Procedural-Rhetoric.title: Procedural Rhetoric
389/Concepts/Procedural-Rhetoric.content:
A term from Ian Bogost: games make arguments through their procedures — through what they let you do, what they reward, what they obscure, what they refuse to let you do. Monopoly argues that ownership is good and renting is bad. The Outer Wilds argues that knowledge is its own reward. Up the River argues that self-interest beats spite.
Reading a game procedurally means asking what worldview is implicit in its rules. Designing one means recognizing that every game says something about how the world works, whether you intended it to or not.

389/Concepts/Prototyping-as-Playable-Que.content:
A prototype is not a product. It’s a test.
Every prototype should be built to answer a specific question: does this core loop work? Does the camera do what we need? Is the art style conveying the right thing? Does this platform support the interactions we want?
If you can’t say what question your prototype is answering, you’re probably building a small version of the final game instead of a tool for finding things out.

389/Concepts/Reusing-Objects-and-Spaces.title: Reusing Objects and Spaces
389/Concepts/Reusing-Objects-and-Spaces.content:
A single object can do many jobs at once. A tower can be a landmark, an objective, a vantage point, and a place to fight — all four. Good level design loads up its elements with multiple functions instead of building one thing per purpose.
Manifold Garden uses architectural detail to orient the player, convey scale, and create traversal challenges. The purple portal in The Talos Principle is both a doorway and the visual goal it tells you to walk toward. Overwatch 2’s Lijiang Tower is landmark + objective + traversal space.

389/Concepts/Revelation-and-Recontextual.title: Revelation and Recontextualization
389/Concepts/Revelation-and-Recontextual.content:
The other way to make surprise land: not the moment of explosion, but the moment of re-reading. The viewer or player has to reinterpret everything that came before based on a new understanding. The Sixth Sense, Fight Club, Bioshock, Spec Ops: The Line, Shadow of the Colossus.
The twist works because it forces a change in perspective. You anticipated one outcome and got something else entirely; the effectiveness comes from how it transforms the characters in your mind.

389/Concepts/Self-Conscious-Emotions.title: Self-Conscious Emotions
389/Concepts/Self-Conscious-Emotions.content:
Emotions that involve reflection on oneself — feelings you have because you’re conscious of your own actions. Games are uniquely positioned to evoke these, since they take your choices into account.

Guilt — the feeling of deserving blame. Spec Ops: The Line, Shadow of the Colossus, This War of Mine.
Pride / Fiero — satisfaction from achievement. Soulslikes; also You Have to Burn the Rope, which gets there without difficulty.
Naches (Yiddish) — the pride a mentor takes in a student. Tamagotchi, Nintendogs, Black & White.
Embarrassment — feeling judged. Lollipop Chainsaw’s deliberately public achievements; party games generally.
Coliberation (Bernie DeKoven) — the feeling of participating in something larger than yourself. A well-played game, even between opponents.

All of them rest on the player believing their actions matter — which is why Agency and Self-Efficacy sits underneath the whole category.

389/Concepts/Show-Your-Process.content:
A potential employer cares about your product, but they care even more about your process. Of course you want finished games on your portfolio — but it’s the explanation of what you contributed and how you work that turns a portfolio piece into a credible signal.
Showing your process gives readers who understand design confidence that you have good practices. It demystifies design for readers who don’t. And it can rescue a portfolio piece that didn’t ship as cleanly as you’d hoped.

389/Concepts/Small-vs-Large-Surprises.title: Small vs Large Surprises
389/Concepts/Small-vs-Large-Surprises.content:
Movie stories are made of a series of surprises, some tiny and some big. A story with only small surprises has dull pacing. A story with only large surprises quickly loses its impact.

Small surprise: the young protagonist… smokes.
Large surprise: the young protagonist… is an alien.

The important surprises are the ones produced by the main character’s actions — which means they’re usually the result of a dilemma. Pacing is the work of stringing small and large surprises together at the right intervals.

389/Concepts/Subtext-and-Theme-via-Metap.title: Subtext and Theme via Metaphor
389/Concepts/Subtext-and-Theme-via-Metap.content:
Subtext is meaning beneath the surface, accessible only when you decipher the metaphor. A metaphor is a comparison between two things that are otherwise unrelated; the qualities of one are figuratively carried over to the other (Tim Jensen, “What is Metaphor?”).
Three scales:

Short metaphor — a single image. The house is a house.
Extended metaphor — runs across several beats. Multiple steps build it up.
Controlling metaphor — extends across the whole work. Papo y Yo’s monster is the controlling metaphor of the entire game.

When metaphors are coupled with puzzles, the player isn’t simplifying — they’re arriving at meaning and making that comprehension their own.

389/Concepts/Sunk-Cost-Fallacy.title: Sunk Cost Fallacy
389/Concepts/Sunk-Cost-Fallacy.content:
The tendency to keep going down a path you’ve already invested in, even when the objectively better move is to abandon it and start over. It’s one of the natural biases that pulls players toward non-optimal choices.
Games can lean into this — sunk-cost pressure is part of what makes risk/reward and progression systems feel weighty — but it can also frustrate, especially when a game punishes a player for cutting losses.

389/Concepts/Surprise-vs-Suspense.title: Surprise vs Suspense
389/Concepts/Surprise-vs-Suspense.content:
Alfred Hitchcock’s bomb-under-the-table distinction:

“Let us suppose that there is a bomb underneath this table between us. Nothing happens, and then all of a sudden, ‘Boom!’ There is an explosion. The public is surprised, but prior to this surprise, it has seen an absolutely ordinary scene, of no special consequence.
Now, let us take a suspense situation. The bomb is underneath the table and the public knows it… In these conditions this same innocuous conversation becomes fascinating because the public is participating in the secret.
In the first case, we have given the public fifteen seconds of surprise at the moment of the explosion. In the second we have provided them with fifteen minutes of suspense.”

Surprise is a single beat at the moment of revelation. Suspense is the long stretch of anticipation that exists because the audience knows something the characters don’t. Games can use either, but suspense is usually the more useful raw material.

389/Concepts/Surrealism-in-Games.title: Surrealism in Games
389/Concepts/Surrealism-in-Games.content:
Surrealism was a European art movement of roughly a century ago. It featured illogic to draw attention to the unconscious mind, and the work of interpretation — turning illogic into a logical meaning — was the viewer’s job.
In games like Papo y Yo, Maquette, Antichamber, Baba Is You, Inside, the player takes on essentially that role. The space presents non-sequiturs and the player transforms them, through play, from unconscious imagery into conscious sense.
The term gets overused in everyday speech — “that was so surreal” — so be careful. Surrealism in games is specifically the structure where illogic is the puzzle and meaning is the player’s reward.

389/Concepts/Tale-Spin-Effect.title: Tale-Spin Effect
389/Concepts/Tale-Spin-Effect.content:
Coined by Noah Wardrip-Fruin (Digital Humanities 2007). The inverse of the ELIZA Effect: a system has rich internal complexity, but its surface output flattens that complexity to the point where the player can’t tell it’s there.
Tale-Spin (1976) modeled characters with goals, plans, and beliefs — but the stories it produced gave you no window into any of that. “No matter how creatively one plays with Tale-Spin, such hidden action cannot be deduced from its surface.” A useful design caution: if your simulation is doing something interesting, the player needs surfaces that show it.

389/Concepts/The-Macro.title: The Macro
389/Concepts/The-Macro.content:
A spreadsheet that lays out every gameplay sequence in your project — name, description, and three kinds of goals:

Player goals — what the player thinks they’re trying to do
Design goals — what the level needs to accomplish mechanically, narratively, otherwise
Experience goals — what the player should feel, beat by beat

Building this grid early forces the team to align on intent. Once the goals are clear, you can fill in mechanics, enemies, puzzles, clues, locations, assets, audio. The macro is the “30,000-foot view” — the document that lets you cut scope before it eats you.
You’ll be asked to make one in nearly every USC Games production class. 489 especially.

389/Concepts/The-Unused-Emotional-Palett.title: The Unused Emotional Palette
389/Concepts/The-Unused-Emotional-Palett.content:
Most games limit themselves to a small handful of emotions: excitement, frustration, surprise, fear, triumph. Designers tend to reach for those by default because the tools to evoke them are well-developed.
But there’s a much wider palette available: longing, awe, melancholy, isolation, romance, giddiness, delight, awkwardness, connection, yearning, discontent, ecstasy, loss, liberation, vulnerability. Many of these have barely been explored. Targeting one is a way to do something fresh.

389/Concepts/Values-at-Play.title: Values at Play
389/Concepts/Values-at-Play.content:
A brainstorming framework (Mary Flanagan and Helen Nissenbaum) for thinking critically about what games communicate — and for designing games that take on themes outside the usual palette. The associated Grow-A-Game card deck uses four decks; in 389 we lean on two of them:

Verbs — game mechanics. What can the player do? Build, match, avoid, trade, tempt, nurture, disarm, bridge, include, redistribute.
Values — what the game rewards. Trust, privacy, sustainability, humility, democracy, style, communication, diversity, equality.

Pick a verb and a value. What might a game look like that used the verb as its core mechanic and expressed the value? Most pairings are productive precisely because they’re not obvious.

389/Concepts/Weenies-and-Landmarks.title: Weenies and Landmarks
389/Concepts/Weenies-and-Landmarks.content:
A “weenie” is Disney parlance for a tall, distinctive visual element that orients visitors across a large space — the Tree of Life at Animal Kingdom, Cinderella’s Castle at the Magic Kingdom. Games use the same trick: St. Mark’s Campanile in Assassin’s Creed II, the mountain in Journey.
Landmarks give the player a stable reference point in a complex space. But for a Lost Woods, you don’t want them to be too oriented — choose your landmarks deliberately, and decide what you’re willing to give away.

389/Lectures/Week-1.1---Course-Introduct.content:

The opening session: course overview, introductions, the Parable of the Clay Pots, the full semester project structure, attendance / grading / AI policies, then the Lost Woods study (mazes in games, from Return to Zork through The Path to Catacombs of Solaris).










CTIN 389 — Course Overview
What to expect from this semester.























Goals for this Course
You will learn the techniques used to solve common design problems. You will apply design thinking in original contexts to express yourself creatively. You will practice the basic skills you learned in previous classes and become more comfortable with them.
By the end of this course, you will have completed several projects demonstrating the core techniques of designing digital experiences and be prepared to tackle a larger project in CTIN 489.

bit.ly/4oRqN1i
In the #introductions channel, post a message:

Your name and pronouns
Three games you know well
Something you’re looking forward to











Parable of the Clay Pots
From David Bayles and Ted Orland, Art & Fear.
A ceramics teacher announced on the first day of class that he was dividing the class into two groups.
All those on the left side of the studio, he said, would be graded solely on the quantity of work they produced; all those on the right would be graded solely on its quality.
For the “quantity” group, he said that on the final day of class he would bring in his bathroom scale and weigh the work: fifty pounds of pots rated an “A”, forty pounds a “B”, and so on. Those in the “quality” group, however, needed to produce only one pot — albeit a perfect one — to get an “A”.
At the end of the semester it came time to evaluate the students’ work and a curious fact emerged: the works of highest quality were all produced by the group being graded for quantity.
It seems that while the “quantity” group was busily churning out piles of work — and learning from their mistakes — the “quality” group had sat theorizing about perfection. In the end the “quality” group had little more to show for their efforts than grandiose theories and a pile of dead clay.










Course Structure — the projects
First half (Unity)

Lost Woods Project (solo) — Due Week 2 — Make an ambiguous space. — attention and direction
Sequencing Project (solo) — Due Week 3 — Create a level sequence with “keys” and “doors.” — triggers and interaction
Racing Project (pairs) — Due Week 4 — Use vehicular movement to make a racetrack. — momentum and artificial intelligence
Quandary Project (pairs) — Due Week 5 — Make an experience that offers a choice. — spatial communication and guidance
Anticipation Project (pairs) — Due Week 6 — Tell a story that ends with a surprise. — user interface and narrative arc
Reinterpretation Project (pairs) — Due Week 7 — Approach a previous prompt from a different angle. — prototyping and iteration

Fall Break — Week 7
Second half (Unreal + exploration)

Unreal Project (pairs) — Due Week 9 — Make a game in Unreal Engine. — engines and technology
Video Game Remake Project (pairs) — Due Week 11 — Remake a previous project in Unreal. — iteration and adaptation
Engine Exploration Project (solo) — Due Week 11 — Make a game in another engine. — tools and affordances
Final Project (pairs) — Due Week 15 — Make a game that expresses an ideology. — learning systems and complex expression











Why so many small projects?
One of the key takeaways from this class is practice scoping small projects.
In the first three weeks of CTIN 489, you will be making a new prototype each week. In this class, we’re going to spend most of the semester doing the same thing so that it will be old hat by the time you have to do it for Intermediate.
None of these one-week projects is going to be highly detailed. They’re all going to be small versions of ideas that you could expand on in more time.
I want you to get good at getting things into engine quickly so that you can make larger projects more effectively in the future.










Weekly Rhythm
Tuesdays — Project Introductions, Playtests
Thursdays — Lecture, Tools & Techniques, Discussion of Readings, Demonstrations, Exercises

Study — Lost Woods
The art of getting lost and finding your way.
When was the last time you got lost?
When I was in college, my parents took me and my sister to Italy and I spent an afternoon with the aim to get lost in Venice.










Mazes — Navigation and Traversal
Video games have a long history of using mazes as obstacles or challenges. But simple mazes are rarely satisfying experiences for players.

Why not?
What makes a maze more satisfying?


Return to Zork (1993) — a 1993 CD-ROM adventure game held in extremely high regard as a product of its time. It contains more than one example of a first-person maze that presents a simple, brute-force obstacle to the player. These mazes suck.
This sort of maze was a popular aesthetic in the mid to late 20th century, akin to the try-and-die dungeon design of OSR D&D like the Tomb of Horrors.
There was a huge secondary market for “strategy guides” and 1-900 tip lines that just compiled maps so that you wouldn’t have to painstakingly draw them out yourself. (King’s Quest V, 1990.)










Lost Woods — the alternative
Mazes-as-mapping-exercises have fallen out of favor in recent decades.
There’s not a lot of nuance to the frustration of not being able to find your way, and there’s not a lot of satisfaction to be had from rote memorization of a safe route.
But there’s another way to think about maze spaces in games, and that’s as a guided experience. Mazes can make players disoriented, but they can also be opportunities to make them feel clever and give them a sense of mastery over a dangerous or mysterious environment.










Ocarina of Time — guiding the player

Ocarina of Time (1998) — Lost Woods.
The Lost Woods in Ocarina of Time aren’t just a maze. The game tells you what to pay attention to and your attention guides you through the space.
You can brute force this puzzle. You can draw or follow a map. But you don’t have to, because the game gives you the tools you need to find your way.
You might feel lost, but the game gives you a path to follow.

389/Lectures/Week-1.2---Lost-Woods.content:
Today’s agenda — Discussion (the Explore/Exploit reading), Unity Review, Ideation & Design (group brainwriting toward the Lost Woods project).
This session opens with a Unity Essentials refresher carried over from CTIN 289, introduces tools for directing player attention, runs a group brainwriting exercise on the concept of “being lost,” sets up Perforce for the semester, and closes with a discussion of the Explore/Exploit chapter from Algorithms to Live By — all leading toward the Lost Woods project assignment due Thursday.
Today’s Agenda
Discussion — Ideation & Design. We’ll talk about the reading and discuss the Explore/Exploit tension.
Unity Review — Let’s do some group brainstorming and talk about making decisions. We’ll go over some essentials you’ll remember from CTIN 289, as well as some 3D-specific topics.
Review of Unity Essentials
Models, materials, lights, etc.
Let’s open up Unity! Download the Essentials assets from the Google Drive.
Unity Version: 6000.0.14f1
Render Pipelines — what are they?
A render pipeline is a package of rendering features built into the runtime.
A pipeline will support certain features (raytracing, LOD, Shader Graph, etc.) and not others. It offers differing levels of platform support, rendering quality, etc.
Render Pipelines — why?
All those extra features must be built into the runtime (the Unity DLL that travels with your build).
The more features, the bigger the build size that your player has to download. Some features can be stripped out at compile time, but not all.
The rendering process will take more CPU and GPU resources to run on your player’s machine. This limits what devices you can target, requires more optimization on your part, and often leads to player complaints if they aren’t using a high-spec machine.
Render Pipelines — the three options
Unity has three common render pipelines:

the built-in option
Universal Rendering Pipeline (URP)
High-Definition Rendering Pipeline (HDRP)

I recommend that you default to URP unless you have a compelling reason to use HDRP.
Universal Render Pipeline (URP) is suitable for all platforms, including mobile, but it doesn’t include certain high-end features like ray tracing and volumetric lighting.
Built-in Pipeline is still supported, but Unity has said they will remove it in the future. It doesn’t offer many benefits over the other options. If you set up your project with the built-in option, you can add another rendering pipeline later, but it’s a pain.
High-Definition Rendering Pipeline (HDRP) does include all the high-end features, but requires a high-powered computer or modern console to run, as well as assets that look good at high resolution.
Importing 3D Models
Models will usually be FBX files that you download from the Unity Asset Store, find online, or export from Maya or Blender.
FBX files usually contain model, material, and texture information. Sometimes they can also contain animations.
If your model shows up as bright pink, it means something is wrong with the material that’s applied to it. You should check the material, texture, and shader for issues.
Manipulating Materials
Materials contain lots of information that determines how an object shows up on screen. The parameters that are available to you are determined by the shader that the material is using, but some of them are common:

Color
Texture (Base Map)
Smoothness
Metallic
Emission

You can copy and modify materials. This is a great way to swap out the texture on a character or object, for example.
Lighting a Scene
There are four types of lights: directional lights, point lights, spot lights, and area lights.
Lights emit light according to their color and intensity. Only “lit” materials will react to lights; “unlit” materials ignore all lighting.
Lights can be controlled by scripts. You can turn them on or off, adjust their color and intensity, or change their direction (for directional and spot lights) and position (for point lights, spot lights, and area lights).
You can control general features of the light in your scene using Lighting Settings (Window → Rendering → Lighting). This will be very useful to you for creating atmosphere and mood in your scene. You can change some of them at runtime using the RenderSettings object.
Here are two short tutorials that will give you a jumpstart in actually using the system:

Unity Lighting Clinic
Light Up Your Game
Exterior Lighting in URP

Playing Audio
Your main camera should have an AudioListener component. To play a sound, you need a GameObject with an AudioSource component.
You can have your audio source be part of another object, in which case you just need to call its Play function in a script. But be careful when you’re destroying an object that might still be emitting audio!
You can instantiate a dedicated audio source and have it play on awake, but if you do that you should make sure it cleans up after itself. You can write a script that will self-destruct once it’s done playing. (That’s a useful one to keep in your cookbook!)
Setting Up a Camera
Align with View. A useful tool for working with cameras is the Align with View command in the GameObject menu.
Every scene comes with a camera already in the hierarchy, but you can add more cameras to your scene. If you do, you should make sure you only have one Main Camera (check the tag on the Camera object) and one Audio Listener.
You can turn cameras on and off using scripts or timelines. It is straightforward to set up split screen, though the logic for supporting gameplay can be more complicated.
Render Textures. You can point a camera at a RenderTexture in order to reflect it in the game world (for example, as a CCTV monitor, a mirror, or a 3D object in the UI).
Creating a Particle System
Unity provides you with a really nice system for creating particle effects using a whole bunch of adjustable options. Particle effects are useful for creating things like sparks, flames, smoke, explosions, sparkles, glows, beams, dust, fog, rain, snow, and sprays.
The best way to get started with particle systems is to find a pre-made effect (for example, on the Asset Store) or a tutorial that does something similar to what you’re looking for, and then go nuts tweaking the values. Once you get used to how particle systems work, you can also create them from scratch using custom textures and behaviors.
Recipe — Falling Leaves
Particle System

Duration: 5
Prewarm: Yes
Start Size: 0.3 to 0.5
Start Rotation: 1 to 360
Start Color: Green

Simulation Speed: 0.5

Rotation over Lifetime — Angular Velocity: -10 to 10
Renderer — Star material
Creating and Instantiating Prefabs
Prefabs are important and offer two distinct advantages.
First, prefabs allow you to create multiple copies of one object, or multiple variations of the same basic object. If you need to make changes to the prefab (by updating the model, adjusting some values, adding a script, or anything else) then all the copies will automatically update as well.
Second, prefabs are stored as separate asset files, which means that it’s much easier for developers to make changes to a scene’s prefabs without causing version control conflicts. When you’re putting together your scene, think about how it makes sense to organize things into prefabs.
Player Attention
How do you get the player to look at something in particular?
Roughly, a viewer’s attention is drawn to the following:

Movement
The brightest object
The most saturated color
An actor’s eyes
The object with the most contrast
Center of frame

Players also pay special attention to:

Threats
Interactables

Here is a breakdown of ways to draw and sustain attention, with a focus on web design (Link).
You can see that many elements are shared. On websites you are usually trying to facilitate an interaction, such as buy, learn, contact, find, and so on. The user is usually oriented to websites in general and knows what task they are trying to accomplish.
In games, the verbs are different, and often the player is (intentionally or not) trying to work out what their task is and what the tools are for accomplishing it. This is often a source of the fun! But it can also frustrate. Use the tools carefully to create the arc you want, from feeling lost to feeling found.
Defining Paths
Here is a discussion of creating paths through a level. It is focused on shooter design, but has a lot of useful tips for creating focal points and sightlines, as well as a useful visualization of player paths through a level that helps identify points of choice and bottlenecks (Link).

GDC 2014 talk on navigation point density — Face, UT2003 (806 total navigation points).
Weenies — orienting the player with landmarks
Don’t forget that you can also use landmarks to help orient the player! But for the Lost Woods, you don’t want them to be too oriented.

Disney’s Animal Kingdom — Tree of Life.

Assassin’s Creed II — St. Mark’s Campanile, Venice.

Journey — the mountain.
Ideation & Design — making your Lost Woods deliberately
Group Ideation — Brainwriting
We’re going to practice a group ideation strategy called brainwriting.
Get into a group of 3–5 with the people around you. Form an approximate circle.
Step 1 — Being Lost. Take 5 minutes to think about the concept of being lost. Here are some prompts:

What does being lost feel like?
How can you make a player feel lost?
What could being lost look like in your Lost Woods project?

Write down some ideas on one side of a notecard. Try to make it legible and sensible — you’re going to give this to someone else to read.
Step 2 — Pass left. Pass your notecard to the person on your left. Read the notes on the card that was just passed to you. Reflect on these ideas. What new ideas do they inspire for you? Flip the card over and write on the back. Keep brainstorming. What else can you come up with?
Step 3 — Finding Your Way. Set that notecard aside and get a new one. Here are some more prompts:

What does finding your way feel like?
How can you make a player find their way?
What could finding your way look like in your Lost Woods project?

Again, write out some notes on one side of your notecard.
Step 4 — Pass right. This time, pass the notecard to the person on your right. Again, read the notes on the card that was just passed to you. Flip the card over and continue brainstorming on the back.
Step 5 — Share. Go around the circle and share what’s written on both of your notecards. Continue brainstorming out loud — but don’t get too far off task. Make sure everyone gets a turn.
Ideation & Design — converging
Ideation is the process of building up ideas. Design is the process of whittling those ideas down again.
Make some decisions. Pick one or two ideas from your brainstorming that seem like they might be effective — or at least interesting. How can you implement them? What do you need to build to try them out?
Keep your scope in mind. You’re going to spend around 6–10 hours on this project. How are you going to spend that time?
Next Time — Review of Perforce
File sharing and version control.
Discussion — Explore / Exploit
Discussion prompts (work down the list):

What did you think of this chapter?
Do you think that you have a bias towards exploration?
Can you identify examples of explore / exploit tensions in games that you’ve played recently? How did you optimize play around these tensions?
How can you use what you know about explore / exploit to improve your game design?

389/Lectures/Week-10.1---Technology-and-.title: Week 10.1 — Technology and Development
389/Lectures/Week-10.1---Technology-and-.content:
A tour through one developer’s ever-changing toolset — and why learning new tools is the real skill.
This session uses my own development history as a case study: the long, messy list of engines, languages, and platforms I’ve worked in over the years. The point isn’t the tools themselves — it’s that technology constantly changes, and the next project asks you to step outside Unity and prove you can adapt.










Playtesting — Unreal Interaction Project
Peer feedback session on the previous assignment.










Design & Technology
Let’s take a look at all the tools I’ve used as a game developer — and this doesn’t even include the ones I used as a web dev.










My History as a Game Developer
I did my undergraduate in German Literature, but I’d taken a few CS classes and taught myself some (rudimentary, at the time) web technologies. After graduating I worked as a technical writer and then as various kinds of web developer. While earning my MFA at Parsons, I built projects in Processing and Flash+ActionScript 3, played with brand-new web APIs like the accelerometer and real-time communication, and made my thesis project in Unity 3.3. Then came a small New York game company (Flash+AS3 for an iOS shooter), a stint as UI/UX designer and lead programmer on an iOS app that mimicked Adobe Illustrator (ReactJS front end, Node.js build, a cloud back end calculating building energy impacts), and an interactive data visualization in d3.js.
Then I came to USC. In the twelve years since, alongside primarily using Unity (plus an iPad LiDAR AR app), I’ve also made a simple Alexa app, extensively customized Twine, written an Inform game, made simple Arduino toys, worked with Unreal and Virtual Humans, and built a React/Java webapp for the IndieCade jury system. I spent a summer on an R&D team prototyping math-learning games for toddlers (Unity on iPads), and built a data-visualization tool using Neo4j (a graph database) and Cytoscape.
Along the way: Walden, a game (2010, originally in the licensed Gamebryo Lightspeed engine, later rewritten in Unity); my MFA thesis Grayline (2011, a co-op detective game for iPad in Flash — which stopped being buildable when Apple changed iOS provisioning); FutureBound (2013, Unity, about navigating middle school); and a run of experimental collaborations with Martzi Campos and Jesse Vigil.
A career’s worth of tools, in pictures:

DarkCon (2005) — VR memory research at ICT; a custom C++/OpenGL engine on networked SGI machines, with a “scent collar.” DOD-funded for five years.

Spectre (2009) — a 2D narrative platformer in Flash/AS3, on a framework by freshman Asher Vollmer (later of Threes). IndieCade Honorable Mention; IGF Student Showcase Winner.

Walden, a game (2010) — built in the licensed Gamebryo Lightspeed engine, later rewritten in Unity.

Grayline (2011) — my MFA thesis, a co-op detective game for iPad in Flash.

FutureBound (2013) — Unity, about navigating middle school and building college-going ambitions.

From Ivan (2018) — an absurd visual novel built almost entirely in Unity’s UGUI, with Martzi Campos.

The Klaxo Radio Hour (2018) — an interactive audio drama built into a physical radio: Unity on a stick PC talking to an Arduino.

ARBox (2019) — AR escape rooms; Unity clients plus a custom PHP/MySQL server driving IoT devices. Featured by Google at GDC 2018.










Technology Changes
That list is the whole point: technology changes, and learning to work with new tools and processes is a critical skill for a game developer. Many studios use Unreal and Unity — but the truth is most use proprietary engines, and even more use plugins, tools, and custom mods you’ve never seen. Having experience with a studio’s specific technology is great, but it’s far more important to be willing and able to learn new things.

389/Lectures/Week-10.2---Procedural-Rhet.title: Week 10.2 — Procedural Rhetoric
389/Lectures/Week-10.2---Procedural-Rhet.content:
How games make arguments and express values — and how documentation holds the production process together.
Two threads run through this session. First: procedural rhetoric — reading games as ideological artifacts, asking what each game is implicitly saying about how the world works. Second: design documentation — the treatment, macro, and specification, and why the macro in particular is the production tool you’ll be asked to make in every USC Games class.










Today’s Agenda

Curation — feedback on ideas and discussion of game precedents.
Design Documentation — using documentation as part of a production process.
Procedural Rhetoric — how games can be used to make arguments and express values.











PSA: Vote!

vote.ca.gov
caearlyvoting.sos.gov
Vote by mail, vote early, same-day registration!











Procedural Rhetoric










Ideology
What does Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic have to say about how the world works?

Knights of the Old Republic — light/dark alignment meter.
How do games represent ideologies?

What aspects of the world are represented?
How are they represented? What are their relationships to each other and the player?
What aspects of the world does the game not bother representing?
What actions are allowed?
What effects do they have? How do they relate to the players and the end states of the game?
What actions are NOT allowed?
What skills, talents, methods, and strategies tend to be rewarded?











Ideology — Up the River (1988)

Up the River (1988) — Ravensburger board game.
What does Up the River have to say about how the world works?

Boats are made to get to a destination.
Persistence is valuable against an environment that resists traversal.
Luck, speed, and sacrifice are rewarded.
It’s better to be self-interested than spiteful.
Only one person can win.











Ideology — Monopoly (1935)

Monopoly (1935).
What does Monopoly have to say about how the world works?

You should try to get as much money as you possibly can.
Ownership and investment are valuable tools for increasing capital.
Paying rent is bad. Collecting rent is good.
Luck and persistence are rewarded.
If you are wealthy, jail is just an inconvenience.
Parking should be free.











Ideology — Fallout 4 (2016)

Fallout 4 (2016).
What does Fallout 4 have to say about how the world works?

The world is divided into civilization and wilderness.
Civilization is valuable but requires constant maintenance and protection.
The wilderness is hostile but it should be explored and looted.
Violence is usually the answer.
Dogs are great.











Ideology — The Outer Wilds (2019)

The Outer Wilds (2019).
What does The Outer Wilds have to say about how the world works?

The universe is full of worlds to be explored and mysteries to be investigated.
Exploration is tricky, but not dangerous.
You don’t know what you don’t know.
Speed, knowledge, and persistence are all rewarded with even more knowledge.
Sometimes it’s nice to sit by a fire with a friend, listen to some music, and toast a marshmallow.











Precedents and Curation
Precedents

Designers work from precedents.
If you can’t find one, keep looking.
A precedent doesn’t always exactly match what you are trying to do.











Curation

A Steam library — your curation source.
What’s in your Steam library that is worth playing? Can you name something from your collection that is:

less than eight minutes to demonstrate what is interesting
available to play in the classroom











Design Documentation
What is the purpose of design documentation?

Who is it for?
Why is it written at the end of pre-production?
What does it need to communicate?

Design documentation comes in three flavors:

Treatment
Macro
Specification











Design Treatment

Wireframe sketches — the kind of artifact a treatment includes.

Overview document
Executive summary
Enough details for someone to understand the basic concept
Diagrams and wireframes

The design treatment is extremely valuable for onboarding and is often used for pitching.










Design Macro

Production document
Spreadsheet
Detailed description of project scope
Lists assets and resources
Easy to reference and update

The design macro is usually an internal resource most useful for production planning.










Design Specification

“Classic” GDD
Reference document
Long-form detailed information
More diagrams, tables, and charts
Also: art bible, world bible, TDD

Design specifications are not popular, because they are difficult to incorporate into an iterative process. When things change, the specification must be updated — which is an onerous task.
That said, design specifications are sometimes needed to show publishers or investors the project at a greater level of detail.










The Macro, in Depth
Let’s talk about the macro. It’s one of the core documentation tools you’ll be asked to create in just about every USC Games production class. (Certainly it will be a major part of 489.)

15 weeks, 4 project phases — ideation, pre-production, full production, post-production.
In the macro, you will describe every sequence of gameplay you intend to build. You will give it a name, a description, and you will detail out the goals of each of these sequences.
There are three kinds of goals for each sequence:

the player’s goals (what the player thinks they are trying to do)
the design goals (what the level needs to accomplish mechanically, narratively, or otherwise)
your experience goals as a director (what the player should feel, beat by beat, as they play through the sequence)

By building this grid, and defining your goals with each specialty in your group, you will find that the macro helps align your team from the very start of the pre-production process. Once you know what your goals are, you’ll be able to fill in your mechanics, any NPCs/enemies, puzzles, clues, locations, other objects and assets that will be needed.
This is your “30,000 foot view” of the project that not only aligns your team, but allows you to scope your effort and make cuts early so that you can manage your resources effectively. The idea behind the macro is that it’s easy to keep it up to date as the design changes.

Designed Experiences — in other media
Designed experiences are media that are created to inspire a particular emotional reaction from their audience.
When you experience any kind of media, think about:

What emotions is this designed to make you feel?
How does it go about evoking those emotions in you?


It’s helpful to think about the words you use to describe emotions. This is one example of an emotion wheel. (There are lots of different variations.) It’s not an especially good model of human emotion, but it is a good place to start looking at vocabulary.

Caught up in adventure

Graphic design
Size

Contrasting the fantastical and the mundane

Screams from ahead

Think of a piece of media that made you feel a strong emotion.
Don’t pick a game or anything game-related.
Write down your name, the piece of media, and the emotion.










Evoking vs depicting
There’s a difference between evoking an emotion and depicting an emotion.
Modern cinematic narrative games often depict characters going through more complex emotional arcs. But for the next assignment, we’re interested in designing a game that makes the player feel a particular emotion, not just the characters.










The unused emotional palette
Most games limit their experience to just a few common emotions. These are things like excitement, frustration, surprise, fear, and triumph.
As a designer, don’t overlook the many other emotions that you can include in your game experience.
For your next assignment, you can either choose the emotion you wrote on your card or one of these alternatives:

longing, awe, melancholy, isolation, romance, giddiness, delight, awkwardness, connection, yearning, discontent, ecstasy, loss, liberation, or vulnerability.

If you choose the emotion on your card, I want you to get very specific. Remember how that piece of media made you feel and target that particular emotion. However, you are not creating an adaptation of that piece of media. The game, story, and context for the emotion should be your own.

389/Lectures/Week-12.2---Evoking-Emotion.content:
A recap of the semester’s four arcs of experience, and an in-class workout analyzing games through them.
This session reviews the four arcs of experience we’ve covered all semester — narrative, mechanics, subtext and theme, and agency — then puts them to work: a head-to-head “Book Club” comparison and a rapid in-class analysis of a long list of games. It closes with the reading that frames the next unit: Tynan Sylvester on games as engines of experience.










The Four Arcs of Experience
Let’s recall the four arcs of experience presented this semester.
Narrative. Stories are about characters who act and change. Characters face difficult choices that spur them to action and force them to reflect. Each choice is an opportunity to surprise the audience, and pacing is made of small and large surprises strung together. Sometimes the dilemma is more interesting than the outcome — we want to wonder what they were thinking.
Mechanics. Mechanics define how the player relates to the player character and the game world. Changing the mechanics causes the player to reevaluate their experience. Mechanics that reflect the character’s experience of the world draw the player into the character’s story; changing them to reflect the character’s choices and growth makes the player invested in the character’s dilemmas.
Subtext and Theme. Games often follow a surrealist pattern of presenting illogic and prompting the player to make meaning out of it. Stories use metaphors to explore complex ideas in novel ways; subtext suggests there is meaning to be found if we work to unlock it, and controlling metaphors serve as the keys. Surrealism asks us to reconcile the conscious with the unconscious, turning it into metaphor and subtext.
Agency. Games let players feel self-efficacy — the belief that their actions make a difference. Agency is subjective: usually we care more about how much the player seems to have than how much they actually do. Self-conscious emotions like guilt, pride, fiero, naches, and embarrassment are based on the player reflecting on their own actions. Games can employ “narrative listening” and use feedback to increase the player’s sense of agency.










Book Club — VS
A head-to-head comparison exercise. For each prompt, weigh the two games on the table against each other:

Which game is most fun?
Which game speaks to the underdog in us all?
Which is best enjoyed with others?
Most style, least substance?
Most substance, least style?
Best dramatic premise?
Best designed objective?
Tells the best story?











In-Class Game Analysis
Work through these games, each paired with an analytical lens. Rotate the lenses across the list — formal/dramatic/dynamic elements, the narrative/mechanical/metaphorical arcs, agency, and the emotions evoked.
A few of the games on the table:

Before Your Eyes (2020).

Gorogoa (2017).

Papers, Please (2014).

Gone Home (2013).


La Madriguera (2021) — What are the formal elements? The rules, procedures, objectives, conflicts?


Thirty Flights of Loving (2012) — What are the dramatic elements? Premise, characters, visual style?


Before Your Eyes (2020) — What are the dynamic elements? How do affordances and constraints create an experience through play?


Dr. Langeskov, The Tiger, and the Terribly Cursed Emerald (2015) — What is the narrative arc? Who is the protagonist and what do they want?


Spaceplan (2017) — What is the mechanical arc? What changes and what stays the same?


Gorogoa (2017) — What is the metaphorical arc? What subtext can be extracted from a close reading of its symbols?


Frog Fractions (2012) — What agency does the game present? What self-reflective emotions does it play with?


Umurangi Generation (2020) — What are the formal elements?


The Roottrees are Dead (2023) — What are the dramatic elements?


Her Story (2015) — What are the dynamic elements?


Reigns (2016) — What is the narrative arc, and how is it presented to the audience?

Papers, Please (2014) — What agency does the game present?


Gone Home (2013), Meteorfall (2020), and others — What are the dominant emotions evoked, and what techniques are used to evoke them?












Two Lenses
Elements of game design (formal, dramatic, dynamic) are one way to construct and deconstruct games. Arcs of experience (narrative, mechanical, metaphorical, self-reflective) are another. How are you using these tools in constructing your prototypes?

Here are some slides from IMGD alum Steven Atha, which he will use in an upcoming level design workshop. Keep an eye on the newsletter.










Reusing Objects and Spaces — Manifold Garden

Manifold Garden — architectural detail in an Escher-style infinite space.
The architectural detail in Manifold Garden:

Creates orientation in a disorienting space
Helps the player understand how large an object is as well as how near or far
Creates a navigation challenge











Reusing Objects and Spaces — Balatro

Balatro — the Amber Acorn boss flips and shuffles all Joker cards.
The Amber Acorn boss in Balatro reorders and hides Jokers (power-up cards) the player has built to work in a sequence. This:

Creates a challenge for the player by disrupting their strategy
Rewards players for paying attention to the shape and size of joker cards
Gives the player a mini-memory game remembering what order the cards trigger in, adding depth to that important mechanic











Reusing Objects and Spaces — Who’s Lila

Who’s Lila — the player must manipulate the character’s face to mimic facial expressions.
The moments in Who’s Lila where your character has to mimic a facial expression emphasize how alienated the player character feels from his peers.
They occur at regular story beats and set the player up for the PC’s increasingly antisocial behavior.










Reusing Objects and Spaces — The Talos Principle

The Talos Principle — the purple portal visible in the first moments.
The purple portal visible in the first moments of The Talos Principle serves as a doorway but also as a visual landmark and objective, telling the player where to go in order to proceed.










Reusing Objects and Spaces — Overwatch 2 Lijiang Tower

Overwatch 2 — Lijiang Tower level.
The tower in the Lijiang Tower level of Overwatch 2 also serves as a visual landmark and objective, while offering opportunities for the player to jump, fly, shoot, etc. and use the specific powers of their character to traverse the open area around it.

389/Lectures/Week-13.2---Cinematics.content:
Today’s agenda — Cinematics (techniques for creating cutscene cinematics in Unity), Portfolios (looking at portfolio pages from students and recent graduates), and the Salmond Reading discussion.
A workshop session: walk through Unity’s Timeline + Recorder for building cutscene cinematics, then look at example portfolio pages from recent students and graduates, then discuss Sylvester’s Engines of Experience chapter.










Interactive Lights and Cameras
Let’s open up Unity! Download and open the Timeline demo project.










Timeline — opening the window
Open the Timeline window and dock it somewhere convenient.

Window > Sequencing > Timeline

I like to dock the Timeline at the bottom of the editor window, along with the Project and Console windows. It’s useful to have a wide space to work with.










Timeline Asset
A timeline needs to be connected to both a GameObject on the Hierarchy and an asset in the project files.
Create an empty GameObject and call it Timeline. When you select it, the Timeline window will prompt you to create the Timeline asset. Save this asset somewhere appropriate in your project folder.










Lock Window View
Once you create your Timeline asset, you’ll want to lock your Timeline window to the Timeline GameObject. (Otherwise, it will try to show a new timeline whenever you select a different GameObject.)
Click the lock icon on the top right hand corner of the Timeline window.










Animation Track
An animation track can change the transform of a GameObject and interpolate between different transform values.
Drag any GameObject into the left side of the Timeline and select Animation Track. For example, you can create an animation track for a camera.
Click on the record button on the animation track to begin recording. Move the playhead to a time on the timeline and adjust the object’s transform to create a keyframe at that point. Move the playhead and create another keyframe, and the timeline will animate between them.










Activation Track
An activation track controls whether a GameObject is active or not.
Drag any GameObject into the left side of the Timeline and select Activation Track.
Right click on the timeline track and select Add Activation Clip. Adjust the starting and ending times of the clip on the timeline. During times when the clip is on the timeline, the GameObject will be active; whenever the clip is not on the timeline, the GameObject will be inactive.










Audio Track
An audio track can control what audio file plays from an Audio Source.
Drag an AudioSource into the left side of the Timeline and select Audio Track.
Right click on the timeline track and select Add From Audio Clip, or drag an audio asset directly into the timeline track. You can adjust the starting point of the track and see how the waveform will line up with other elements on your timeline. Remember that you can only play one audio file from an Audio Source at a time.










Unity Recorder
One more thing: Unity has a native recorder component that you can use to capture frames or video of your game. You have to download and install the Recorder package from the package manager, but it’s very easy to use.
Once you’ve installed the recorder, you can open the Recorder window from:

Window > General > Recorder > Recorder Window

When you start the recorder, it will automatically enter play mode and play your game. The recording will stop when you exit play mode. You can also set the recorder to automatically exit play mode if you end the recording from the Recorder window.
Add a new recorder. Make it a Movie Recorder. Check the settings. It will default to the same resolution as the Game window and save the video to a Recordings folder at the top level of your project.










Activity — Make a Cinematic
In small groups, use the Timeline and post processing effects to create a small cinematic cutscene. You should animate the camera and some lights.
You can use any assets you have access to, or grab some from www.kenney.nl/assets/category:3D.
Record your cinematic using the Unity Recorder and post it to the Discord.










Portfolios — approach as a design problem
A portfolio is interactive media! Approach your portfolio as a design problem, the same way that you would approach designing a game.
First step: What’s your experience goal? Think about what you want someone to understand about you when they look at your portfolio.
How can you present your work to create that understanding?










Portfolio examples
Michael Ford — Digital Design, Tabletop Design, Sound Design
Melody X Wang — www.melodyxwang.com/
Celine Tang — celinetang.com/games
Meny Menczel — www.menymenczel.com/
Thomas Lu — thomastianlu.com/










Flip the script
We don’t often talk about it in these terms, but flipping the script is a vital design skill. As a game designer, you have to think about what your game looks like to a brand new player. You’ve developed the skills to put yourself in that person’s shoes, even though you know a lot more about the game than they do.
Put yourself in the shoes of the person who’s looking at your portfolio. What do they want? What are they looking for? How much time are they going to spend looking at your website?
Use role-playing and playtesting to help get into the head of a reviewer!










Show your process
A potential employer is not just concerned with your product; in fact, they care even more about your process. Of course you want to put games that you’re proud of up on your portfolio, but it’s important that you explain what you contributed to the game and how you do your work.
Show your process. This will give readers who understand design confidence that you also have good practices. It also demystifies design for readers who don’t have a lot of experience with these processes. And it can help turn a lackluster product into a valuable selling point.










Discussion — Experience Engines
Thoughts on making players feel things.
Discussion prompts:

What did you think of this chapter?
Do you agree that detecting and understanding subtle emotions is a designer skill? Do we value it appropriately?
Did any of Sylvester’s emotional triggers stand out to you, as particularly resonant or unjustified? (Emotion through learning, character arcs, challenge, social interaction, acquisition, music, spectacle, beauty, environment, technology, primal threats, and sexual signals.) Is this list complete?
How does emotional variation relate to your current prototypes?
